catalog_quote: In Paresi, word stress has delimitative functions in that it indicates word boundaries. In general, stress occurs in the penultimate syllable of a word. Acoustically, vowel duration may be the main correlate of stress. [...] Paresi exhibits a penultimate stress pattern, as shown in (71), contrary to the analysis in Silva (2013) where stress is not predictable in monomorphemic words. There are few trisyllabic and polysyllabic noun stems (without any suffixes) and they also follow this pattern. [...] (71) a. toto ['to. to] 'breast' b. kafaka [ka.'fa.kɐ] 'yesterday' c. tihanare [ˌti.ha.'na.re] 'sorcerer' [...] However, there are exceptions to this stress pattern. Some words receive stress on the last or antepenultimate syllable. This case can be explained by syllable weight. Paresi exhibits quantity sensitivity, in which stress falls on a heavy syllable with two moras: CVV, as shown in (72). (72) a. kotyoi [ko.'tʲuj] 'tapir' b. irai [i.'dʲɛj] 'he told' c. alatai [a.la'.tai] 'cascudinho fruit' c. ferakoa [fe.ra.'koa] 'in the morning' d. kaimare ['kai.ma.re] 'moon' e. wainama ['wai.na.mɐ] 'be. tasty'
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.locator: pp. 55-57 (pp. 78-80), §2.5.1 'Stress patterns'; summary statement also p. 4 ('Stress is generally not contrastive, and stress assignment depends on syllable weight and number')
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (480 pdf pages; title page: "A reference grammar of Paresi-Haliti (Arawak)", Ana Paula Barros Brandão, University of Texas at Austin, May 2014, supervisor Patience Epps). extracted text of pp. 78-80 (printed pp. 55-57) gives §2.5 Prosody / §2.5.1 Stress patterns; every sentence of the reported quote is present word for word: "In Paresi, word stress has delimitative functions in that it indicates word boundaries. In general, stress occurs in the penultimate syllable of a word." (p. 55); "Paresi exhibits a penultimate stress pattern, as shown in (71), contrary to the analysis in Silva (2013) where stress is not predictable in monomorphemic words." (p. 56); "However, there are exception…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the stress domain (root plus stress-bearing suffixes; proclitics, prefixes and the suffixes -ti, -ta, -nae, -ne, -re do not count); a heavy CVV syllable (diphthong) attracts stress away from the penult (to the final or antepenult); a handful of nouns have lexically final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words with more than three counted syllables get a secondary stress two syllables before the primary (e.g. [ˌθe.ko.'ha.tse.ti] 'leader'); a heavy syllable can also attract secondary stress ([i.ˌdʲai.he'ne.re]); suffixes -kala, -hare, -hena carry their own penult stress (pp. 60-61).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with a heavy CVV syllable take stress on that syllable (final or antepenult: kotyói 'tapir', káimare 'moon'); five noun pairs contrast penult vs final stress (máka 'night' / maká 'hammock', etc.); a few irregular items (ohíro 'woman', hinamá 'two', ezanityó 'wife', ezanené 'husband'); proclitics, prefixes and the suffixes -ti, -ta, -nae, -ne, -re are outside the syllable count, while -kala, -hare, -hena carry their own penult stress; monosyllabic stems are bimoraic (minimal-word requirement). Silva 2013 (pp. 101-110) analyses stress in monomorphemic words as purely lexical and polymorphemic words as iambic, which Brandão explicitly rejects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; data elicited in carrier sentences (not isolation forms) because phrase-final pitch rise in isolation can be perceived as final stress; stress is described as delimitative (marks word boundaries) and 'generally not contrastive' (p. 4).
new_statements.identity_note: Brandão 2014 and Silva 2009/2013 describe Paresi-Haliti (ISO pab, Glottolog pare1272) of the Chapada dos Parecis, Mato Grosso; Brandão's data come mainly from the Waimare and Kozarini sub-groups (aldeias Formoso etc.); no separate dialect glottocode is involved.

new_statements.translation: p. vi: 'Column-3 prefixes: the 2sg prefix is not stressed, whereas the 3sg prefix is stressed. E.g. hawénakala "your village" and háwenakala "his own village".' p. i: '[ə] variant of a, often in the syllables ka and na in the stressed syllable, as in cama'; '[ɪ] sometimes in the stressed syllable before k'; '[ɨ] in the stressed syllable with h, l, k, x'. Headword pairs: káli 'frog sp.' / kalí 'to bear fruit'; káxoko 'to please' / kaxóko 'easy to'; káxiye 'ungenerous person' / kaxíye 'confused'; kóre 'opossum' (also kóre1 'tall grass') / koré 'arrow'; wátyaha 'to be waiting' / watyáha 'dove'.

(under the possessive-prefix paradigm table where 2sg col.3 = ha- and 3sg col.3 = ha-); headword p…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Brandão 2014 statement (penultimate default, quantity-sensitive, 'a few pair of nouns' where stress alone contrasts, with final stress in the second member): Rowan's kóre 'gambá' / koré 'flecha' is exactly Brandão's pair (73c) [ˈko.re] 'opossum' / [ko.ˈre] 'arrow', and the practice of accenting only contrastive pairs fits a predictable default. Adds pairs not in Brandão's list (káli/kalí, káxoko/kaxóko, káxiye/kaxíye, wátyaha/watyáha) and a morphological stress contrast on the ha- possessive prefix (2sg unstressed vs 3sg stressed) that the catalog does not record. States no placement rule itself, so it neither confirms nor contradicts penult vs Silva 2013's lexi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary and its grammar sketch state no rule for where word stress falls. They presuppose a stressed syllable (allophone conditioning 'na sílaba tônica'), state one morphological stress contrast (possessive prefix ha- 2sg unstressed vs ha- 3sg stressed: hawénakala vs háwenakala), and write an acute accent on headwords only for a handful of pairs distinguished by stress alone (penult vs final in disyllables: káli/kalí, kóre/koré; initial vs medial in trisyllables: káxoko/kaxóko, káxiye/kaxíye, wátyaha/watyáha), which implies stress is otherwise predictable enough to leave unmarked but lexically contrastive in a few items.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-only minimal pairs marked with acute accents (káli/kalí, kóre/koré, káxoko/kaxóko, káxiye/kaxíye, wátyaha/watyáha; isolated accented forms éxanene 'marido', enéxe 'cheiro', hóka 'quebrar', iyó, atyoá 'peneira', wománe); 2sg vs 3sg ha- prefix distinguished by stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Rowan 2001 is a dictionary of Paresí (autodenomination Haliti), Mato Grosso, c. 500 km NW of Cuiabá, compiled 1960-1998 with speakers from many villages; no dialect is named in the front matter (Rowan 1964, per Silva 2009 p. 106, distinguished a Kaxiniti/Waimaré remnant from the majority Kozarini, but this dictionary does not say which it represents).

sources.citation: Silva, Glauber Romling da. 2013. Morfossintaxe da língua Paresi-Haliti (Arawak). PhD thesis, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro. 603 pp.
sources.note: §2.4 Acento, pp. 101-110: 'Em palavras monomorfêmicas, o acento é puramente lexical' (no predictable pattern); polymorphemic words show a bidirectional syllabic iambic pattern (one iamb at the left edge, then iambs from the right); primary stress on the rightmost stressed syllable; nominalizers -re, -lo, -ze, -ro, collective -nae, plural -ha and perfective -tya are lexically stressed, -ti is the only unstressed suffix; no stressed prefixes/proclitics; §2.4.2: in suffixed words measured in isolation the highest pitch coincides with primary stress on the last syllable.

sources.citation: Silva, Glauber Romling da. 2009. Fonologia da língua Paresi-Haliti (Arawak). MA thesis, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (orient. Bruna Franchetto). 22+319 ff.
sources.note: §3.12.2 pp. 190-198 (metrical analysis, impressionistic): minimal word is disyllabic; 'a grande maioria das palavras em Paresi são paroxítonas'; in polymorphemic words stress is attracted to the last syllable of the last suffix (tóna / tonitá, etiníhi / tinihití); emphatic pronunciation lengthens the first syllable and shifts stress to the final (óne ~ o:né); a final diphthong attracts stress (kotyói). §3.3.3 pp. 86-87: long vowels non-phonemic, mostly in the penult of words with final stress.

sources.note: Codes the language as having no suprasegmental phonemic features (field 'Suprasegmental: None', i.e. no tone, no contrastive stress listed, no phonemic nasal harmony), compiled from Silva 2013, Brandão 2014 and Rowan 2001. Secondhand but the only explicit 'no tone' statement located for Paresi; the primary sources themselves describe weight-sensitive/penultimate stress and phrase-final pitch raising without ever raising tone as a possibility.
